cards.front: A {{c1::watershed}} is all the land that drains into one river, lake or bay.
cards.quote: A watershed is all the land that drains into one river, lake or bay.
cards.section: From a watershed to bottom water

cards.front: {{c1::Runoff}} is rainwater that flows over the ground instead of soaking in, carrying what it picks up.
cards.quote: Runoff is rainwater that flows over the ground instead of soaking in, carrying what it picks up.
cards.section: From a watershed to bottom water

cards.front: Water too low in oxygen for most animals, usually below 2 mg/L, is {{c1::hypoxia}}; in the Chesapeake Bay it forms mostly in bottom water.
cards.quote: Water too low in oxygen for most animals, usually below 2 mg/L, is hypoxia; in the Bay it forms mostly in bottom water.
cards.section: From a watershed to bottom water

cards.front: {{c1::Eutrophication}} is the enrichment of water with nutrients, which feeds too much algae growth and can lead to oxygen loss.
cards.quote: Eutrophication is the enrichment of water with nutrients, which feeds too much algae growth and can lead to oxygen loss.
cards.section: From a watershed to bottom water

cards.front: What is dissolved oxygen, and in what units is it measured?
cards.back: Oxygen gas mixed into water, measured in milligrams per liter (mg/L).
cards.quote: Dissolved oxygen is oxygen gas mixed into water, measured in milligrams per liter (mg/L).
cards.section: From a watershed to bottom water

cards.front: Put the steps of eutrophication in order, from extra nutrients to low-oxygen bottom water.
cards.back: Extra nutrients, algal bloom, algae die and sink, bacteria decompose them and use oxygen, low-oxygen bottom water.
cards.why: The fertilizer never takes oxygen itself; living things use it.
cards.quote: extra nutrients → algal bloom → algae die and sink → bacteria decompose them and use oxygen → low-oxygen bottom water
cards.section: From a watershed to bottom water

cards.front: No one pours an oxygen-absorbing chemical into the Chesapeake Bay. What actually uses up the oxygen in a summer dead zone?
cards.back: Bacteria, as decomposers, use oxygen while breaking down dead algae that sank to the bottom.
cards.why: Fertilizer feeds the algae but does not take oxygen itself.
cards.quote: bacteria decompose them and use oxygen
cards.section: From a watershed to bottom water

cards.front: Why can scientists forecast each summer's dead zone in the Chesapeake Bay from spring river data?
cards.back: The chain from nutrients to bloom to decomposition takes months, so the nutrients rivers carried in spring set up the summer's oxygen loss.
cards.quote: Because the chain takes months, scientists forecast each summer's dead zone from the nutrients rivers carried in spring.
cards.section: From a watershed to bottom water

cards.front: In the Chesapeake Bay, a storm mixes the water layers before the nutrient supply changes. What happens first to oxygen near the bottom?
cards.back: It rises. Mixing brings oxygen-rich surface water down before the dead algae change.
cards.why: The closed-room picture of bottom water breaks down when a storm opens the door.
cards.quote: A storm mixes the layers before the nutrient supply changes. What should happen first to oxygen near the bottom?

cards.front: In a shallow, nutrient-rich cove, is oxygen lowest near sunset or just before sunrise?
cards.back: Just before sunrise. At night algae stop photosynthesis but keep using oxygen, so oxygen can drop very low even in shallow water.
cards.quote: At night algae stop photosynthesis but keep using oxygen, so oxygen can drop very low even where the water is shallow.

cards.front: An ecosystem's capacity to support life depends on which four things?
cards.back: Habitat, light, oxygen and food.
cards.quote: An ecosystem's capacity to support life depends on habitat, light, oxygen and food.
cards.section: People and nature both change ecosystems

cards.front: How can burning fuel in cars and power plants, or ammonia gas from manure and fertilizer, add nitrogen to a watershed?
cards.back: Nitrogen falls from the air onto land and water.
cards.quote: Nitrogen falls from the air onto land and water
cards.section: People and nature both change ecosystems

cards.front: A wildfire burns a forested slope above a Virginia stream. What happens to the stream after later storms, and why?
cards.back: More ash and soil wash into the stream. Storms afterward carry them down from the burned ground.
cards.why: A natural event can change what reaches an ecosystem, as human land clearing does.
cards.quote: Storms afterward wash ash and soil into streams
cards.section: People and nature both change ecosystems

cards.front: A farm stops adding fertilizer this year. Will the nitrogen in its runoff drop to near zero right away? Why or why not?
cards.back: Probably not. Some nitrogen is stored in the soil and leaks out years later, so responses lag.
cards.quote: Extra nutrients, some stored in soil and leaking out years later
cards.section: People and nature both change ecosystems

cards.front: In designing a watershed fix, what is the difference between a criterion and a constraint?
cards.back: A criterion is what a solution must achieve, such as cutting a set amount of nitrogen. A constraint is a limit such as money, land or time.
cards.quote: Criteria are what a solution must achieve, such as cutting a set amount of nitrogen.

cards.front: A town plan must cut nitrogen by a set amount and can use only the money in its budget. Which is the criterion and which is the constraint?
cards.back: Cutting the set amount of nitrogen is the criterion. The budget is the constraint.
cards.quote: Constraints are limits such as money, land and time.

cards.front: How does a riparian forest buffer reduce nitrogen reaching a stream?
cards.back: Its plants and soil microbes remove nitrate from water seeping through the ground. Its roots also hold the bank.
cards.why: How much it stops depends on its width, soil and water flow.
cards.quote: Its plants and soil microbes remove nitrate from water seeping through the ground.

cards.front: What is submerged aquatic vegetation, and why does the Bay's ecosystem value it?
cards.back: Underwater grass, usually rooted in shallow bottoms; it shelters young crabs and needs light.
cards.quote: It shelters young crabs and needs light.

cards.front: A 2018 study of the Chesapeake Bay found that as nitrogen in Bay water fell, underwater grass regained about 17,000 hectares. What does this suggest?
cards.back: Cutting nutrients can help habitat recover. It is evidence of a link over time, from nitrogen falling to grass returning.
cards.quote: A 2018 study found that as nitrogen in Bay water fell, underwater grass regained about 17,000 hectares, roughly 42,000 acres.

cards.front: In the Bay Program's model, nitrogen load was 297.1 million lb per year in 2009 and 252.7 in 2025. By what percent of the 2009 load did it fall?
cards.back: Drop = 297.1 - 252.7 = 44.4 million lb per year. 44.4 / 297.1 is about 0.149, so about 15 percent.
cards.quote: What percent of the 2009 load is that, and how much more must it fall to reach the goal?

cards.front: The 2025 modeled nitrogen load is 252.7 million lb per year and the goal is 219.5. How much more must it fall, as a percent of the 2009 load of 297.1?
cards.back: 252.7 - 219.5 = 33.2 million lb per year. 33.2 / 297.1 is about 0.112, so about 11 percent of the 2009 load.
cards.quote: What percent of the 2009 load is that, and how much more must it fall to reach the goal?

cards.front: Underwater grass in areas mapped in both years was 76,835 acres in 2024 and 82,968 acres in 2025. What was the percent change?
cards.back: Gain = 82,968 - 76,835 = 6,133 acres. 6,133 / 76,835 is about 0.080, so an increase of about 8 percent.
cards.quote: Grass areas come from the VIMS 2025 preliminary survey.

cards.front: Why compare underwater grass only in areas mapped in both years?
cards.back: So the change reflects the grass itself, not a different amount of area surveyed.
cards.quote: Why compare grass only in areas mapped in both years?

cards.front: Does the Bay Program's modeled nitrogen load report the nitrogen rivers carried in one wet or dry year?
cards.back: No. It estimates what the practices do under average weather.
cards.quote: It does not report the nitrogen rivers carried in one wet or dry year.

cards.front: If modeled nitrogen load to the Chesapeake Bay falls, must modeled hypoxic volume fall in every following year?
cards.back: No. River flow, temperature and wind vary, so yearly oxygen estimates can bounce even while nutrient pressure falls.
cards.quote: River flow, temperature and wind vary, so yearly oxygen estimates can bounce even while nutrient pressure falls.

cards.front: Modeled nitrogen loads fell, yet 2024's hypoxic volume (497 km³·days) was about two and a half times 2023's (199). Name two things besides nutrients that could explain this.
cards.back: River flow, temperature or wind. Two years are too few to judge a trend or test a cleanup.
cards.quote: Two years are too few to judge a trend or test a cleanup.

cards.front: Buffer and control trays leave the same nitrate concentration in runoff, but the buffer tray makes less runoff. Did the buffer reduce nitrate leaving the tray?
cards.back: Yes. Nitrate leaving equals concentration times runoff volume, so the same mg/L in less water means less nitrate left.
cards.quote: The nitrate leaving equals concentration times runoff volume, so the same mg/L in less water means less nitrate left the tray.

cards.front: In a fair tray test of a grass buffer, what is the independent variable, and what are the dependent variables?
cards.back: Independent: buffer strip or no buffer strip. Dependent: nitrate in the runoff (mg/L) and runoff volume. Soil, slope, fertilizer amount, water poured and waiting time are held constant.
cards.quote: Independent variable: buffer strip or no buffer strip.

cards.front: In a buffer tray test, results from buffer and control trays overlap. How could you refine the test, and what are the limits of trays as a model?
cards.back: Widen the strip, add trays or try another plant. Trays are a model, not a stream: they test only water flowing over the surface, while a real buffer also works underground.
cards.quote: If results overlap, widen the strip, add trays or try another plant.

cards.front: In a model of the Chesapeake Bay, warming cancelled about 6 to 34 percent of the oxygen gain from cutting nitrogen. Would cutting nitrogen still help oxygen, and why does warming matter?
cards.back: Yes, most of the gain remains. Warmer water holds less oxygen and speeds oxygen use, so warming offsets part of the gain.
cards.quote: In one computer-model study of the Bay, warming cancelled roughly 6 to 34 percent of the oxygen gain from cutting nitrogen.
cards.section: A law, a model and a distant disturbance

cards.front: A county reduces runoff for ten years and sees one bad low-oxygen summer. How should it judge whether its cleanup is working?
cards.back: Judge over years, not one summer. Weather makes single years bounce, so look at whether nutrient pressure, habitat and oxygen move over time.
cards.quote: Judge them over years, because weather makes single years bounce.

cards.front: A county wants to cut nitrogen and bring back underwater grass. Give a plan order that follows the Chesapeake Bay rule, and say why.
cards.back: Cut nutrients first, then rebuild habitat such as underwater grass and reefs, then track recovery over time. That is the order the Bay rule gives.
cards.why: Rests on the rule: effective fixes cut nutrients first, rebuild habitat, and track recovery.
cards.quote: effective fixes cut nutrients first, rebuild habitat, and track recovery over time.
